1965 Ferrari 275 GTS Spent Over 40 Years in Hiding, Sells for Nearly $1 Million
10 photos
Photo: Christie's
Ferraris are some of the most desirable classic cars out there, with many of them worth millions of dollars . They usually get pampered a lot. However, while many of them reside in museums and fancy collections, others have been hidden from sight for decades. This 1965 275 GTS is one such vehicle.
This Ferrari was recently auctioned off via Christie's at Retromobile New York Auctions. It crossed the block in late November 2026. The event marked its first public appearance in over four decades. And despite not being driven for so long, the 275 GTS is still in pretty good condition, especially for an unrestored survivor.
Although it didn't have a rough life, this Italian drop-top didn't get a lot of maintenance either. The iconic red paint is faded, weathered, and even cracked in places, with some surface rust visible on the trunk lid, the nose, and the lower sides.
The soft top is quite dirty as well, while the door panels look like they haven't been cared for since the car rolled off the showroom floor. The interior could use new carpets, while the tan seats need a much-deserved cleaning. Everything else appears to be fine, though; I haven't spotted cracks on the dash and steering, and there are no missing bits and pieces to run by.
As for the V12 engine, it's as original as they get, and it has plenty of dust and grime to brag about. Much like the interior, this engine bay hasn't been detailed. The car crossed the block with a few extra parts, including a front end, bumpers, headlamps, and chrome trim.
It's unclear if the car was originally shipped to the US, but existing documents show that it's been on this side of the Atlantic since 1979. That's when it was purchased by Ferrari enthusiast Charlie Kemp. He sold it later that year to a gentleman named Richard Watkins, who kept it in Richmond, Virginia until 1980.
Then it found its way to another Ferrari enthusiast, Barbour Byrd Wilson, who kept it in Hudson, Wisconsin, from 1980 to 2006. The previous owner kept it for two decades, until the Ferrari changed hands at the recent New York auction.
Speaking of which, the Ferrari was estimated to fetch between $1 million and $1.2 million, but it eventually sold for $995,000. The sum likely includes a buyer's premium.
Introduced in 1964 as a replacement for the 250 GTO, the Ferrari 275 series spawned models like the GTB, GTS, GTB/4, and the GTS/4 NART. Several cars were modified for racing.
The GTS was a convertible version of the GTB , but it had quite a few unique features, including a shorter front hood and smaller uncovered headlamps. Mechanically, it was virtually identical to the GTB, but the 3.3-liter V12 engine was slightly less potent at 260 horsepower. Ferrari produced only 200 units between late 1964 and early 1966.
Examples in excellent condition typically go for seven-figure sums. As of this writing, the five most expensive 275 GTS models fetched between $1.87 and $2.36 million. Three units fetched over $2 million since 2025.
